title: The Mystery of the Dim Lanterns
markdown:
Dawn cracked over Sparklebrook in pink and gold. Festival Day. In the town square, the magnificent Prism Lanterns — meant to be the jewels of the night — sat stubbornly dim. Grey. Not the show anyone had been promised.

Rafi the young technician tapped his chin, fingers twitching. Beside him, Cora the jackdaw surveyed the lanterns with a critical tilt. Her obsidian feathers gleamed; her eyes missed nothing.

"They're just not sparkling, Cora. Imagine grey lanterns all night."

Ms. Lin, who kept the Curiosity Shop in a riot of silks and stones, sighed. Even her brightest ribbons looked a little subdued. "Light should be bursting, Rafi, not hiding. Remember what I told you? It isn't always just plain white. It has colours tucked inside."

Rafi nodded. She had shown him sunlight kissing a dewdrop and bursting into a miniature rainbow. "Splitting light," he whispered.

Cora hopped to a giant unlit lantern and pecked the thick clear glass. "Caw. Dark." Then a single morning beam struck a dewdrop on the pane. For a fleeting second, a faint rainbow flickered.

"Wait." Rafi's eyes widened. "That dewdrop is splitting the light." He ran his fingers over the smooth glass. "Ms. Lin said sunlight is all the colours mixed. This plain glass is a door with no trick on it. White goes in, white comes out, and it looks grey against the square."

Cora jabbed her beak at a crumpled scrap of red cellophane from last year's decorations. Rafi held it to the weak sun, then to the lantern glass. The beam that emerged was only red. Deep. Simple. Not a rainbow.

"That's a filter," he said, excitement climbing, and then a little too far. "So we put filters on, then prisms, and the prisms will split that red even further and make it brighter—"

Ms. Lin's mouth tipped, dry as good ribbon. "A prism will not unpack red into a rainbow, dear. Red is already a single note. A prism needs the whole chord — white light — to fling a spectrum. The cellophane is for when you want one colour on the cobbles. The prism is for when you want the hidden mix to show."

Rafi's worry vanished in a more useful direction. "So the glass is fine. We need two jobs. Filters for solid colour. Prisms for rainbows. Not one after the other as if they were the same tool."

"I have just the bits," Ms. Lin said. "Discarded decorations, old lenses, waiting for a new purpose."

Cora zipped overhead as messenger. They cut squares of red, deep blue, sunny yellow. They found small triangular prisms. Rafi taped cellophane to some panels, each colour its own section, and set prisms in the white paths — the unfiltered glass — where sun could hit them clean.

As the sun climbed, a beam struck a prism first. Colour exploded across the cobbles: a proper spray, dewdrop-logic made large. Another beam went through red cellophane and laid a clean crimson wash, smelling, Rafi insisted, faintly of berries, though Cora looked unconvinced. Yellow became a gold pool. Blue, a stripe of sapphire. No one had asked the prism to invent extra red, and it had not.

Townspeople gasped. Laughter. Cheers. Cora swooped through the beams, dark feathers catching sparks, and cawed as if she had designed the sun.

Rafi wiped grease from his cheek and told a knot of wide-eyed children the truth, which was better than the first idea. "Sunlight is a mix. A prism spreads that mix — dispersion — the way a dewdrop does. A coloured filter lets one part through and swallows the rest. That's why the lanterns were grey: they were honest, and honesty isn't a show. Now they sort the light on purpose."

The festival had its jewels. Cora circled high.

Rafi looked at the dewdrop, already gone from the glass, and at the prisms still working.

"I wonder," he said to Ms. Lin, "whether tonight's candle-flame, which isn't as white as the sun, will make a weaker rainbow — and whether we'll need the filters more after dusk, when the mix isn't as rich."

Ms. Lin's eyes twinkled. "A technician who asks about evening light," she said, "may borrow the shop ladder. After the square has had its cheer."
